title: Jobs killed at the wall clock
technical_category: Timeout kills (not already in an array/hardware incident)
explanation: 1,541 jobs ran past their time limit and were killed, destroying the work already done. Roughly half of that is avoidable with better time-limit sizing or checkpointing -- the rest may be genuinely under-provisioned, not waste.
evidence: sum(metadata.impact_gpu_hours) over the 1,541 of 1,544 wallclock-kill findings whose job_id is not already claimed by the hardware-attributed-failures or failed-job-arrays category
methodology_note: Recoverability is genuinely mixed: some jobs need a longer time limit (not waste, mis-provisioning), others are hung/stuck work that a checkpoint or a timeout-aware restart would recover. The 45-80% range reflects that split, not measurement error.

title: GPUs booked but never touched
explanation: 1,098 jobs held a GPU for their entire run and never used it -- either they crashed before doing any real work, or they succeeded without ever needing a GPU. The most clear-cut waste in the cluster.
evidence: sum(metadata.impact_gpu_hours) over the 1,098 jobs where sm_util_avg AND sm_util_max were 0.0 for the job's whole life -- gpu-never-computed (did not COMPLETE) and gpu-not-needed (COMPLETED on CPU only) partition by outcome and share zero jobs by construction
methodology_note: Highest-confidence category: deterministic telemetry (avg AND peak both exactly zero), unambiguous fix (fix/kill the failing job, or stop requesting a GPU for CPU-only work).

title: Running jobs holding more GPU than they use
technical_category: Running but inefficient (low utilization / oversized memory / imbalance)
explanation: 763 jobs did real work but used only a sliver of the GPU capacity they reserved, or left one card idle next to a busy one. Rightsizing recovers some of this; the job's underlying compute need is often real, so this is the least recoverable category.
evidence: 763 distinct jobs across 4 utilization detectors, deduped by taking one detector's metadata.impact_gpu_hours per job (precedence: multi-node > low-util > mem-oversized > imbalance) where a job trips more than one (measured overlap: 24/63 multi-node also low-util, 21/63 also slow-cancel)
methodology_note: Job did real work, just inefficiently -- not eliminable, only rightsizable (fewer GPUs, bin-packing, a fractional-GPU queue). Lowest recoverable fraction of any category.

title: Idle jobs nobody noticed for hours
explanation: 607 jobs sat idle for hours before someone cancelled them. A faster automated liveness check or notification would recover part of the wasted hold time -- but not all of it, since some of that time is a person legitimately still reviewing.
evidence: sum(metadata.impact_gpu_hours) over the 607 of 949 findings not already claimed by the gpu-never-used category (311/949 overlap with gpu-never-computed, excluded there)
methodology_note: Measures detection latency, not utilization. Cannot distinguish a hung job from one whose owner stepped away -- a liveness check recovers the former, a notification the latter; range assumes anywhere from a third to two-thirds is recoverable.

title: Machines sitting below 20% for weeks
explanation: 35 machines ran below 20% utilization for three or more consecutive weeks. Consolidating their workload onto fewer machines could free this capacity, but has real switching/migration cost.
evidence: sum(metadata.impact_gpu_hours) over 35 node-weeks-in-breach findings across 35 distinct nodes -- node-scope, no job_id join, kept as its own pool
methodology_note: Business-decision threshold (20%), not a statistical anomaly. Recoverable only via consolidation/decommissioning, which has switching cost the range reflects.

title: Jobs lost to a machine that was actually broken
explanation: 31 jobs were lost to machines the scheduler recorded as failed, or that causal analysis independently confirmed were broken (one machine kept receiving work for a week while 140 of 144 jobs on it failed). Deliberately a small number -- most failures are not hardware.
evidence: sum(metadata.impact_gpu_hours) over node-failure (31, scheduler-recorded NODE_FAIL, failed-attempt hours only) + node-hardware-fault (1 incident, causally attributed to r216287-n200569 via POST /v1/causal, score 1.0)
methodology_note: Deliberately small by design -- this is the only real, scheduler+causal-confirmed hardware evidence in the corpus. A team reporting a small number here is reading the data correctly.

title: Shared storage slowdown (illustrative scenario)
explanation: An illustrative shared-storage slowdown scenario -- NOT real MIT telemetry -- that models 121 machines running degraded for a 48-hour episode. Kept separate and clearly flagged; must not be blended into real-savings totals.
evidence: sum(metadata.impact_gpu_hours) over all 121 node-level rows of the one episode (confirmed via POST /v1/causal: all resolve to pvc/scratch-lustre-02, score 0.88, fs p99 latency +30.3x, 121 nodes)
methodology_note: This is the one synthetic scenario in the whole corpus (metadata.synthetic = true on every row) -- a MantisGrid-generated scenario, not real telemetry. Confidence is capped low for that reason regardless of the rule's own reported confidence.

title: Interactive sessions left open and idle
technical_category: Idle interactive sessions (residual, not already GPU-never-used/array/hardware)
explanation: 235 interactive sessions were left open and idle for hours after the person stopped using them. An automatic idle timeout on interactive allocations would recover nearly all of this.
evidence: sum(metadata.impact_gpu_hours) over the 235 of 906 idle-interactive-session findings whose job is not already claimed by gpu-never-used, timeout-kills, or failed-job-arrays (528/906 overlap with gpu-never-computed, 109 with gpu-not-needed, 268 with wallclock-kill)
methodology_note: Near-total recoverability: an idle-timeout policy on interactive allocations eliminates essentially all of this by construction.

title: Batch job arrays that failed almost entirely
explanation: 149 batch job arrays failed almost entirely -- usually one bug in the array's script affecting every copy. Fixing the root script once, rather than each of 5,044 failed individual task findings, recovers this.
evidence: sum(metadata.impact_gpu_hours == metadata.gpu_hours_lost) over the 149 array-mass-failure records (one per array, >=10 tasks & >90% failed) -- NOT the 5,044 array-task-failure findings, which are the same incident's individual tasks (rootCauses -> the array)
methodology_note: 5,044 task-level findings collapse to 149 real incidents. Summing the task-level findings instead would inflate this ~34x.
